data.title: Google picks Bezos' Blue Origin to launch AI computing satellites in 2029
data.description: Nov 19 : Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin said on Thursday that Alphabet's Google had selected its New Glenn rocket to launch satellites for Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space. The planned mission advances efforts to move power-hungry AI computing beyond Earth, using sunlight in orbit to ease pressure on electricity grids, land and cooling systems. Companies including Elon Musk's SpaceX and startup Starcloud are exploring data centers in orbit as growing AI use drives demand for computing capacity and strains infrastructure supporting facilities on the ground. The launch, targeted for the first quarter of 2029, will be Google's first heavy-lift flight dedicated to Project Suncatcher and will carry several computing satellites aboard New Glenn. Each satellite will carry Google's tensor processing units, the search giant's in-house chips built to run AI programs, with computing capacity roughly equal to a rack of servers in a conventional data center. They will enter an orbit that provides near-continuous sunlight, allowing Google to examine whether solar energy can support intensive computing in space. Thursday's agreement gives Blue Origin a major future mission for New Glenn as the company seeks to expand its launch business following delays and a launchpad explosion in May. Google and Planet Labs launched the first Project Suncatcher prototype aboard a SpaceX rocket in October and said the satellite was operating as expected after establishing contact. That mission is testing whether the chips can withstand launch forces, radiation and extreme temperatures, while engineers study how to cool them without the airflow available on Earth. Radiation can damage electronics and corrupt data, while heat from powerful chips must be released through pipes and panels rather than conventional cooling systems. Experts have also noted that high launch costs, engineering hurdles and limited satellite production can put data centers in orbit years away from commercial use.

data.title: UK tribunal confirms government order demanding access to Apple data
data.description: LONDON, Nov 19 : The British government has issued an order to bypass encryption to access customer data held by Apple, a London tribunal confirmed on Thursday, rejecting an argument that revealing its existence could damage national security. The government had said that it could not comment on the existence of the order, known as a technical capability notice, because it operated a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" on security matters. However, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal said the amount of information already in the public domain meant that confirming it would do little, if any, damage. There was no immediate comment from the British government or Apple. Campaign group Liberty, which challenged the government alongside Privacy International, called the ruling "a victory for transparency". FIRST ORDER DROPPED AFTER US INTERVENTION In January last year, Britain issued an initial notice for what is known as a back door to allow it access to encrypted cloud backups of data of US and British citizens. That demand was dropped following months of ​negotiations with US President Donald Trump's administration, but in July Britain issued a second notice that applied just to Apple's UK customers. Apple launched a renewed challenge against the government at the tribunal, a specialist court, but had been unable to give public details on why because of legal restrictions. Civil rights groups and Apple had told the tribunal at a hearing in September the British government's "neither confirm nor deny" policy was an affront to open justice and prevented meaningful public discussion. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal said in its ruling that the government "has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that (Britain's interior ministry) has given Apple a technical capability notice." Thursday's ruling was merely to consider whether the notice could be publicly acknowledged and a trial to decide the substance of the case is not expected until next year. The tribunal said it had also handed down private judgments which could not be disclosed without "damaging the public interest". UK SAID CONFIRMATION WAS RISKY The British government's lawyer had argued abandoning the "neither confirm nor deny" stance posed a national security risk and would "provide material assistance to hostile actors." However, lawyers for Privacy International and Liberty said the refusal to confirm the order's existence had become "farcical" after US politicians and officials publicly referred to the original order and unnamed UK government sources confirmed it. The tribunal agreed, citing media reports in the Times and the Financial Times newspapers which it said appeared to have come from "private media briefings provided by government officials". Akiko Hart, director of Liberty, said in a statement: "The public deserve to know when the government's actions undermine their privacy and safety, and we welcome the tribunal's decision, which will shine more light on these secretive powers." The tribunal said that "the extent to which, if at all, the details of the government's notice could be disclosed without damaging national security or the public interest" would be dealt with at a later date.

data.title: JPMorgan says third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
data.description: Nov 19 : JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Thursday that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. "There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week," the spokesperson added.

data.title: Dollar dips as investors pause on Anthropic debut
data.description: Nov 19 : The US dollar index edged down on Thursday after a seven-session winning streak but remained underpinned by hawkish remarks from a Federal Reserve official that reinforced the case for further rate hikes. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a more aggressive response to inflation, while minutes of the central bank's October 27 to 28 meeting showed policymakers increasingly concerned that additional tightening might be needed.  The dollar rally started on November 10 when hotter-than-expected US inflation data bolstered expectations that the Fed would raise borrowing costs next month.  The dollar index this week reached its highest level since April 2, 2025, when US President Donald Trump revealed a sweeping tariff package, triggering a selloff in US assets. It was last down 0.05 per cent at 103.73, after reaching 103.97. Barclays analysts said fiscal stimulus and strong AI-related capital spending point to a resilient US economy, a wider output gap and higher-for-longer interest rates, all supportive of dollar strength. The dollar's gains have come despite a selloff in technology shares. "First, the market has also repriced a more hawkish Fed given recent commentary pushing the interest rate differential wider, but the dollar seems to be overshooting this move," said George Saravelos, global head of forex strategy at Deutsche Bank, explaining the recent rise. "Second, and more intriguingly, foreigners have been very aggressive buyers of US equities even as the stock market has tumbled," he added. A Deutsche Bank tracker following more than 100 foreign-domiciled exchange-traded funds showed large dip-buying of US stocks by foreigners over the last two weeks, the biggest buying spree so far this year. Such a move reinforces the view that the dollar has been supported by investor flows into US equities. Shares in Nvidia fell overnight even after the chip bellwether beat revenue and guidance forecasts, amid uncertainty caused by co-founder Jensen Huang's sudden departure as CEO last week following his admission of extramarital affairs. SAFE-HAVEN FLOWS BOOST THE YEN The dollar was up 0.25 per cent to 159.75 yen, snapping a four-day losing streak. Analysts said that a further selloff in AI-linked assets could support the yen through safe-haven buying and repatriation flows, with the impact likely to be more pronounced against other currencies than against the dollar. According to Barclays estimates, a 10 per cent decline in the S&P 500 from its peak could push dollar/yen towards 155, while a 20 per cent decline could pressure it towards 152. The euro was up 0.34 per cent versus the Japanese currency at 175.43, after falling about 1.5 per cent since late last week. The Aussie dropped as low as $0.6662 for the first time since January. Australia's employment fell for a second straight month in October and the jobless rate climbed to a five-year high, bolstering the view that rates have likely peaked. Following the data, UBS economist George Tharenou brought forward his forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut to August next year from November, and extended the easing cycle to three cuts from two, citing elevated inflation and a deterioration in the labour and housing markets.

data.title: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack through use of AI tools
data.description: BRUSSELS, Nov 19 : The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by a cyberattack through the use of AI tools, although it said that it was difficult to judge the scale of the incident given that an inquiry was underway. "I can confirm that the Commission has recently taken necessary steps in response to a detected cybercampaign," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said at a press briefing.  "As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since been restored," he added. "The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps, based on the findings as they come." "This was an AI-generated cybercampaign," said Regnier.  The incident was detected on October 22 and there was no evidence of any data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, Regnier said. He declined to say who the Commission thought was behind the attack, and said he was not aware of any ransom demand following the incident. The attack on the Commission is the latest high-profile cyberattack, after hacks knocked out commercial refrigerators and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets in October, ships bound for the United States in August, US water treatment plants in July and the Los Angeles transit system in March.  Separately, an hourslong nationwide ground stop in the United States and outages to banking and Microsoft applications were blamed by tech experts on attempts to rapidly patch newly identified software vulnerabilities.  Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission was targeted by a cyberattack which might have compromised large amounts of personal data, with several systems, including HR systems for payslips and time management and a system for medical reimbursements, taken offline during the 10-day disruption. The Commission convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed other commissioners on Wednesday, according to Politico. Virkkunen's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: Anthropic's historic debut to put AI's promise and peril on Wall St trial
data.description: Nov 19 : Anthropic's record $81 billion IPO puts to the test Wall Street's faith in the AI boom, pitting promises of the technology as an economic game-changer against fears of a market bubble and existential risks. More immediately, the Claude chatbot maker securing a $1.5 trillion valuation in an upsized IPO, together with Tuesday's earnings report by AI poster child Nvidia, signals the industry has nominally passed the two big tests facing it this week. Shares in Anthropic were up about 20 per cent in over-the-counter grey market trading, brokerages IG Markets and CMC Markets said. The strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech selloff offers hope to a sector where euphoria has somewhat cooled in recent weeks. "I've looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI. Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies," Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion, said before the Anthropic debut. AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-center-skeptic Democratic tsunami in the US midterm elections. Investors who once embraced the boom have turned skeptical in recent weeks over concerns that the enormous spending needed to build out the sector and the mounting debt loads may not be justified by the eventual returns. Futures tracking the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index climbed early on Thursday, as investors geared up for the much-anticipated debut. AN INDUSTRY BENCHMARK As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with its arch-rival OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing. The company sold 980 million shares at $83 each, pricing the IPO above its initial range of $70 to $78 set when it launched the road show. The additional $26 billion raised through a private placement takes the total haul to over $107 billion. AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet's Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC were the investors in the $26 billion private placement. "Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain," IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer said. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive demand from index-tracking funds will account for about 28 per cent of Anthropic's shares offered, or roughly $19 billion. When it debuts on the Nasdaq later on Thursday, Anthropic will join the trillion-dollar club stacked with behemoths such as Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia. The listing will also give retail investors a chance to pile into one of the AI industry's hottest names, potentially amplifying swings in the stock as trading begins. The buzz has already spilled onto prediction markets, where traders are placing bets on everything from its opening pop to where the stock will close on its first day. JUSTIFYING THE PRICE TAG Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, CEOs and political leaders split over its sustainability. Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fueled by money circulating within the same ecosystem. Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying. "Anthropic is a one-trick pony. People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won't have that luxury," said Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners. "They've got to get to profitability soon." Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, underscoring how its rapid growth hinges on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control. Investors will be watching Anthropic's debut and subsequent trading closely, with analysts expecting the stock to emerge as a proxy for the broader AI trade as questions over valuations, spending and returns weigh on sentiment. The company will also need to balance growth with calls to slow the development of advanced AI models over concerns that they pose cybersecurity threats and could be exploited by bad actors to target critical government and private infrastructure. Anthropic warned in its IPO prospectus that AI could behave unpredictably and advance faster than oversight mechanisms, posing potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

data.title: France's OVHcloud launches AI cloud products hosted in Europe
data.description: Nov 19 : OVHcloud said on Thursday it had launched 55 cloud-computing and AI products that run on infrastructure hosted in Europe, including access to Nvidia's latest AI chips and a workplace application combining email, documents and videoconferencing with AI assistants. The French cloud provider said its data centres could take up to 60,000 of Nvidia's Blackwell chips, a capacity it said matched the largest global platforms. OVHcloud also announced partnerships with cloud-computing company Shadow, Qwant and EUSP, a joint venture between Qwant and Ecosia that develops a European search index. Qwant and OVHcloud said that AI-generated summaries appearing in the search engine's results would be powered by OVHcloud's Olala model and hosted in European data centres. The move comes as European governments and companies increasingly scrutinise where AI services are operated and how their data is handled, creating opportunities for regional providers seeking to compete with US cloud and AI firms.

data.title: Accenture launches plan to cut 950 Meta-linked jobs in Portugal
data.description: LISBON, Nov 19 : Accenture said it aims to cut about 950 jobs in Portugal by January through a voluntary exit scheme for staff serving Meta Platforms, as the Facebook owner pursues an efficiency drive linked to artificial intelligence. • Accenture said it had informed teams in Lisbon providing Trust & Safety services for Meta of the plan to cut about 16 per cent of its Portugal workforce, citing "major changes in client demand for this work and our need to make significant workforce reductions" • The move comes as Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, pursues a broader efficiency drive linked to artificial intelligence • Reuters reported in May that Meta was planning an initial round of about 8,000 job cuts globally as it ramps up AI investment • Accenture said that after assessing the take-up of this offer, it will determine what further steps are required to restructure its teams • It also said it remained committed to Portugal and would continue investing in strategic capabilities and partnerships with Portuguese clients

data.title: Hackers access financial data of retired NYC government workers, Politico reports
data.description: Nov 19 : Hackers accessed the financial information of as many as 4,000 retired New York City government workers this fall after infiltrating an online database created to pay out court settlement fees to retirees, Politico reported on Thursday, citing records obtained by the outlet and a person with knowledge of the matter.

data.title: At COP31, Venezuela touts AI as path to cleaner oil production
data.description: ANTALYA, Turkey Nov 19 : Venezuela is using artificial intelligence to make its oil and gas industry more efficient and curb its environmental footprint, part of a strategy to expand fossil fuel production rather than phase it out, the country's new vice minister for AI and hydrocarbons told Reuters. "Our policy is not to stop producing hydrocarbons," Albania del Mar Villarroel Gomez said on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. "Our goal is to reduce waste and emissions while maintaining energy production." Villarroel said Venezuela is using AI to monitor emissions and methane leaks and improve oilfield operations, reflecting the country's argument at the UN climate talks that technology can help reconcile continued fossil fuel production with efforts to limit its environmental impact. Venezuela's oil and gas sector is among the world's most polluting. Its upstream methane emissions intensity is nearly six times the global average, according to the International Energy Agency. It is the only major energy producer in Central and South America that has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. The approach puts Venezuela firmly on one side of a central dispute at COP31, where countries remain divided over how the summit's final agreement should address a transition away from fossil fuels. Venezuelan officials have defended the country's right to exploit its resources as part of its economic recovery. PRODUCTION PUSH The US military captured Venezuela's former leader Nicolas Maduro in January, and Washington — which is shunning international climate cooperation under President Donald Trump — has since pushed a policy to ramp up the country's oil production. Venezuela pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to figures the government reported in OPEC’s October Monthly Oil Market Report. State oil company PDVSA has said it plans to bring output to 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year. Earlier this year, Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez created Villarroel's post, naming her vice minister for artificial intelligence and productive efficiency in hydrocarbons within the Ministry of Popular Power for Hydrocarbons, which oversees the country's oil, gas and petrochemical sectors. Villarroel said Venezuela plans to focus on smaller, specialized AI models rather than the energy-intensive hyperscale systems developed by major technology companies because tasks such as emissions monitoring, methane detection and oilfield optimization require less computing power. She said the computing infrastructure would be powered primarily by Venezuela's hydroelectric system, which she said supplies about 80 per cent of the country's electricity. Asked whether international technology companies were interested in working in Venezuela, Villarroel said the country had been approached by several companies but declined to identify them. "There is a lot of interest," she said, adding that Venezuela would prioritize protecting national data and maintaining what it calls data sovereignty.

data.title: Binance says Asia expansion plans remain on track after US$6.3 billion hack
data.description: SINGAPORE: Binance said its plans to obtain five additional licences in Asia remain on track despite the recent US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) hack that hit the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, with three licence applications at an advanced stage.  While Binance has faced intense scrutiny after the cyberattack three weeks ago, it has since covered all losses resulting from the theft and says all affected customers have been fully compensated . Binance's head of Asia-Pacific SB Seker told CNA on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday (Nov 18) that the company's handling of the incident had demonstrated its ability to manage operational risks.  He added that Binance has no plans to scale back its Asia expansion strategy following the hack, noting that the “five (licences) are still on track”.  “Out of the five (more licences), three are in very mature stages, and I would say they are quite imminent,” he said. “The conversations with regulators have been fascinating because we've gotten really good feedback that we handled this crisis management in the way they expected us to.” While Mr Seker did not identify the planned markets, Binance currently holds operating licences in more than 10 markets globally.  He has said South and Southeast Asia are key priorities for the company. Further details of its planned expansion are expected to be unveiled in the first quarter of 2027. Binance has been seeking licences across Asia as regulators tighten oversight of the sector and more markets introduce licensing requirements for digital asset service providers.WITHDRAWALS STABILISED Mr Seker acknowledged that withdrawals surged in the immediate aftermath of the cyberattack but had since tapered off. “There was obviously a spike in withdrawals, but that stabilised largely over the last couple of days,” he said. “We're seeing net inflows again.”  Mr Seker added that Binance had replenished a significant portion of its reserves used to cover losses and that the heist did not disrupt day-to-day operations.GREATER FOCUS ON CYBERSECURITY MEASURES The hack has renewed focus on cybersecurity risks facing crypto platforms and the growing sophistication of attacks targeting the sector. Binance linked the incident to North Korean hackers who used fake job interviews and malicious software.  Since then, the company has tightened internal controls, strengthened wallet-risk frameworks and increased its use of artificial intelligence tools to detect threats. “A lot of these threat vectors are AI-driven to begin with,” Mr Seker said. “We're starting to use AI much more to detect these threats much more quickly.”  He added that Binance has also been working with partners in both the crypto and AI sectors to prepare for what it expects will be an ongoing wave of increasingly sophisticated attacks. Despite the incident, Mr Seker noted that demand for digital assets remain strong across Asia, including Singapore.  He said: “Singapore continues to be a major growth driver. If you look at retail, within the age brackets of 18 to 25, 25 to 36, the level of interaction with crypto is steepening … so it's a market we watch very closely.”ROLE OF STABLECOINS  The hack also thrust stablecoins – cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a stable value relative to another asset – into the spotlight, with issuers playing a key role in helping contain the fallout.  “We were able to step in very quickly and freeze about US$1.1 billion that was associated with that hack,” Mr Kash Razzaghi, chief commercial officer of Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin that is pegged 1:1 to the United States dollar, told CNA. The intervention highlighted how stablecoin issuers can play a crucial role in limiting the fallout from major crypto security breaches. While blockchain transactions can be completed within seconds, issuers of some stablecoins can freeze assets under certain circumstances, helping authorities and companies respond to security breaches.  Mr Razzaghi said the incident underscored the need for stronger safeguards across the industry, adding that many major crypto thefts stemmed not from flaws in blockchain technology itself but from human error and social-engineering attacks. “In many cases, these hacks are actually less about the technology and more about missteps in terms of the hackers coming in and building relationships and bypassing protocols,” he said.

data.title: Osaka Gas to expand US, India business despite global geopolitical risks
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 19 : Japanese gas utility Osaka Gas will continue expanding its businesses in the US and India despite rising global geopolitical risks, President Masataka Fujiwara said on Thursday. • Osaka Gas produces and sells US shale gas to domestic customers, and is expanding sales of domestically produced natural gas and renewable energy development in India • The company is not concerned about securing liquefied natural gas supplies for the peak winter demand season as it has no contracts requiring shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and has secured most supplies under long-term contracts, Executive Officer Sunao Okamoto said • However, lower-than-usual European gas inventories could lead to competition between Europe and Asia for spot LNG after the winter, potentially pushing up prices, Okamoto said • Osaka Gas decided to exit the Greater Sunrise gas project, whose gas fields lie between East Timor and Australia, after participating since 2000, as development had made little progress and it was time to move on as part of a portfolio reshuffle, Okamoto said • In September, Osaka Gas bought a 5 per cent stake in Australia's Browse gas project. Okamoto said the company expects the project to eventually move forward and values Australia as a Japanese ally with no major shipping chokepoints. The project would also allow Osaka Gas to secure LNG on a free-on-board basis from its own equity production • Osaka Gas has long-term LNG contracts with Australia, the US, Papua New Guinea and Russia, after contracts with Malaysia, Brunei and Oman expired in recent years. Its LNG transaction volume reached 12.4 million metric tons in the financial year that ended March 2026, with 20 per cent coming from its equity investments in upstream gas projects
